rows.B: DTC Strategy, Loyalty Strategy and UX/UI Design.
rows.C: Helping Rabanne strengthen its direct-to-consumer business while staying true to its luxury positioning.
rows.E: In 2024–25, Rabanne wanted to strengthen its direct-to-consumer business while navigating a familiar luxury challenge: to make digital commerce more effective without making the brand feel overly transactional. The brief was especially interesting because Rabanne operates across beauty and fashion: two categories with very different customers behaviours, purchase rhythms and expectations of the brand.
rows.F: Rabanne could not rely on one generic luxury eCommerce journey. Beauty needed clarity, education, replenishment, loyalty and repeat engagement. Fashion needed aspiration, scarcity, editorial storytelling and brand elevation. From a UX and brand strategy point of view, the challenge was to create a digital experience that could flex between conversion and desire without flattening the brand.
rows.G: The goal was to define a clearer DTC strategy and value proposition for Rabanne, then translate it into a practical roadmap for CRM, loyalty, product discovery, storytelling and eCommerce enhancement. The work needed to identify the moments that mattered most, prioritise the right opportunities and turn them into actionable product and design improvements.

1.- EMPATHISE

Stakeholder and creative interviews to understand business goals, tensions and ambitions

<R_2>

I began by getting close to the people behind the brief. I led stakeholder interviews across Rabanne’s product, CRM, commercial, leadership and creative teams to understand what the business needed, where teams were already aligned, and where there were gaps or competing priorities.

This was not only about gathering requirements. It was about sensing the wider ambition of the project: what Rabanne wanted DTC to do for the business, how beauty and fashion teams understood the role of digital differently, and what kind of experience would feel commercially effective without compromising the brand’s luxury perception.

The interviews helped surface both practical needs and strategic tensions. Beauty required accessibility, education, replenishment, personalisation and loyalty. Fashion required aspiration, scarcity, editorial storytelling and protection of brand equity. This gave the project a clearer foundation before moving into strategy or design.   During the playback of findings i used conceptial diagrams to focus the attention on the main takeaways. This allowed teams to trust our work and judgement moving forward.

<R_3>


2.- RESEARCH

Competitor and market review to understand luxury commerce behaviours and category expectations

<R_4>

I reviewed competitors across luxury, beauty, fashion and premium digital commerce to paing a picture of how other brands were approaching DTC growth, product discovery, loyalty, storytelling and conversion.

The research looked beyond interface patterns. It helped benchmark the value customers were getting elsewhere, from beauty brands supporting education, replenishment and loyalty, to fashion brands using scarcity, storytelling and product presentation to protect desire.

By mapping these category value propositions against Rabanne’s own brand value, uncovered through stakeholder interviews, we built a clearer picture of the brand’s total value proposition.    My hypothesis in a nutshell:  Total value proposition = Category value proposition + Brand’s unique value proposition.

The findings were presented as key highlights, experience opportunities and case studies on top competitors. This helped frame Rabanne’s opportunity: not to copy best practice, but to build a smarter experience that responded to different customer expectations while still feeling like one Rabanne world.


3.- IDEATE

Value proposition and creative workshops with Rabanne’s beauty, fashion and digital teams

<R_5>

Once the initial insight was clear, I led strategic workshops with Rabanne’s client teams to explore the future role of DTC across beauty and fashion. These sessions focused on value proposition design, opportunity mapping, creative ambition and analisys of existing data.

The aim was to help the teams move beyond individual feature requests and consider what the digital experience needed to stand for. We explored what value the platform should create, which customer moments mattered most, how loyalty and CRM could support the journey, and how product discovery could feel more inspiring, useful and brand-led.

The workshops also created space to understand Rabanne’s creative direction and internal coordination between workstreams. This was important because the work could not be purely functional. It needed to translate commercial goals into an experience that still felt expressive, desirable and true to the brand.

From these sessions, a clearer creative ambition emerged: to bring a stronger sense of movement, tactility and sensorial depth into the digital experience. These ideas came from a close reading of Rabanne’s own codes, its materiality, futurist spirit and history of challenging fashion convention, and helped shape how new DTC features could feel both commercially useful and unmistakably Rabanne.

<R_6>

<R_7>


4.- LEADERSHIP ALIGNMENT

Leadership playbacks to build confidence, alignment and momentum

<R_8>

Throughout the process, I created leadership playbacks to share the emerging direction with Rabanne’s senior teams. A leadership review and alignment session was carried at Rabanne’s headquarters to educate, clarify and build confidence around the approach before committing to any further work.

I presented the key findings, strategic opportunities and logic behind our recommendations, including how Rabanne could use the duality between beauty and fashion more intelligently. Beauty offered a lower entry point into the brand’s luxury world, while fashion carried higher exclusivity and equity. This created opportunities to move high-value beauty customers towards accessible fashion moments, and to use beauty as a softer entry point for fashion customers with lower purchase frequency.

The work also clarified the role of a new loyalty programme. How It could support beauty, CRM and repeat engagement, while also creating pathways into fashion, without making loyalty feel central to the luxury fashion experience.

This helped turn the work from a set of recommendations into an agreed DTC direction. The recommendations were presented to Rabanne’s leadership team in Paris and received extremely positively, helping unlock a second phase focused on enhancing their existing digital platform.


5.- STRATEGISE

DTC strategy, value proposition framework, KPIs, ROI model and implementation roadmap.

<R_9>

With the direction aligned, I translated the findings into a strategic framework for Rabanne’s DTC future. This included the go-to-market, value proposition, experience principles, KPI and ROI model, loyalty plan and CRM recommendations, and a prioritised roadmap of digital enhancements.

A key part of this work was the KPI framework itself. Rather than relying solely on standard commerce metrics such as traffic, conversion and revenue, I designed a measurement model that reflected the intended behaviours and value exchanges within the experience. This would later allow Rabanne to assess not only whether customers converted, but how they engaged across the journey through indicators such as gift retention, happy referrals, happy account users, community participation, product consideration and advocacy. By connecting business outcomes to specific experience goals, the framework created a more nuanced view of performance and a practical way to understand which interventions were driving meaningful impact at each stage of the funnel.

Another key part of the work was defining how emerging technologies could strengthen the DTC proposition. Rather than treating AI and Web3 as standalone innovation initiatives, I mapped them against customer behaviours, experience stages and business goals to identify where they could create meaningful value.

This created a clear point of view on the future role of technology within the Rabanne experience. AI was positioned as a way to make the brand more adaptive, personalised and responsive to individual customer needs. Web3 was explored as a way to strengthen authenticity, ownership, participation and trust. Together, these technologies were framed as new relationship-building capabilities rather than features to deploy in isolation.

The framework gave Rabanne a practical way to prioritise future investments and became the foundation for AI and Web3 exploration briefs, helping accelerate internal conversations around how new technologies could support both commercial growth and long-term brand value.

<R_10>


6.- CONCEPTUALISE

Future-state experience vision across beauty, fashion, loyalty and product discover

<R_11>

I then translated the strategy into a set of future-state experience journeys designed around Rabanne’s most important customer archetypes.

Rather than focusing on individual screens or features, these journeys showed how value, storytelling, loyalty, personalisation and commerce could work together across an end-to-end experience. Each journey combined conceptual thinking with visual UI elements to make the strategy tangible without getting lost in design details.

For example, a beauty loyalist replenishing products needed convenience, recognition and timely rewards. A fashion elite customer expected exclusivity, editorial discovery and elevated treatment. A value-conscious shopper responded to referrals, loyalty benefits and social proof. Mapping these journeys helped reveal where Rabanne should behave differently for different audiences, while still feeling like one brand.

The goal was not to redesign the platform. It was to demonstrate how the experience could create stronger engagement, encourage repeat purchase, protect luxury equity and provide a clearer blueprint for future design, CRM and loyalty initiatives.


7.- PRIORITISE

Experience audit, design system review and sprint planning

<R_12>

For the second phase, I audited Rabanne’s existing eCommerce experience and design system to understand what was already working, what needed refinement, and where the biggest opportunities sat.

I identified the modules, content, UX improvements, technical enhancements and design system updates needed to deliver the strategy. I conducted further prioritisation workshops with key members of Rabanne’s digital team, and together built an updated view of the modules list, and work needed into clear design sprints, balancing impact, feasibility and business value.

This ensured the work stayed focused. Rather than trying to reinvent the full platform, we concentrated on the enhancements most likely to improve storytelling, product discovery, loyalty and conversion without disrupting the overall brand experience.


8.- PROTOTYPE

Schematics, content hierarchy, wireframes and Figma prototypes to guide the design team

<R_13>

To move from strategy into execution, I created schematics, wireframes, content hierarchies, interaction models, mockups and prototypes in Figma and After effects.

These tools helped make the thinking visible, and its engagement value easy to perceive. They showed how content should be structured, how modules should behave, how customers should move through the experience, and how different parts of the journey could support both inspiration and conversion.

The prototypes also gave the design team a clearer foundation to work from. They were not only UI outputs, but strategic guidance that translated the roadmap into practical design directives.


9.- DESIGN

Hands-on creative direction and design support through mockups, feedback and reviews

<R_14>

As the work moved into design development, I was still hands-on supporting the design team hands-on through direct feedback, high fidelity Figma sketches, direction for transitions, animations and micro-UX features, to make sure we delivered on the creative ambition, as defined in previous creative workshops with the client, where they asked to incorporate sensorial enhancements with a subtle sense of movement on scroll among other look & feel details that like a natural evolution to the existing art direction.

My role here was to help the team bring the wireframes and strategic intent to life, delegating where oportune or intervening with fined-tuned directives on motion and layout coreography,  making sure the experience did not become too functional, too generic or too detached from Rabanne’s brand world.

This included guiding decisions around hierarchy, UX copy, narrative integrity, interaction, product presentation and overall experience flow. The focus was always to make the work feel useful, desirable and commercially effective at the same time through a sense of rigor, resonance and restrain by flexing the body language of the brand and its iconic sensorial materiality.


10.- TEST

KPI framework, experience hypotheses and usability response direction

<R_15>

While the client’s specialist research team conducted the usability testing, I helped define what the experience needed to prove. I created the KPI framework and a set of experience hypotheses to assess how the proposed enhancements could translate into better customer behaviours and stronger business performance.

For example, one hypothesis explored whether treating gifting as a premium service, rather than a checkout feature, could increase customer confidence, gift conversion and future gift retention. This linked the design direction directly to measurable behaviours such as deeper product consideration, purchases of gifts, repeat gifting and higher average order value.

I also turned the KPI framework into a live online performance tool, built with support from agency developers from the data team and connected to Rabanne’s Google Analytics platform. This allowed the team to view the current experience through a conversion funnel in real time, creating a live benchmark for what was working, where the experience was underperforming, and how future design improvements could be measured in the second phase.

This gave the testing team a more strategic lens. Rather than only validating usability in a functional sense, the hypotheses helped assess whether the experience was improving the right behaviours: clearer product discovery, stronger engagement, better guidance, increased confidence, loyalty consideration and more effective conversion.

During the final design sprints, when the client team came back with questions and findings, I led the response from our side. My role was to interpret the feedback, provide clear UX and design direction, and help the team turn usability insights into practical design solutions without losing the strategic intent of the work whilst avoiding incurring into scope creeps.


11.- IMPLEMENT

Development sprint support, motion feedback and micro-UX refinement

During implementation, I supported the delivery process by reviewing development tickets on JIRA and their sandbox outputs, giving feedback across sprints and helping finesse the details of the experience.

This included notes and conversations to further guide motion, responsive layouts, content treatment and the relationship between modules. 

This final stage was important because the quality of a luxury digital experience often lives in the small details: how something moves, how it responds, how it guides, how it reassures and how it converts without feeling overly transactional.
rows.M:
<R_16>

This project reinforced that successful luxury eCommerce is rarely about adding more features. It is about understanding where commercial goals, customer needs and brand equity intersect, then improving the moments that matter most.

The work gave Rabanne a clearer direction, opportunities, recommendations, frameworks, hypotheses, a roadmap of enhancements, and final designs that delivered on all of it. The strategy was well received by Rabanne’s leadership team and led directly into a second phase focused on product and experience design.

While the project cannot be directly credited for Rabanne or Puig’s wider commercial performance, it sat within a strong business year for the group. Puig reported record FY2025 net revenue of €5.04bn, up 7.8% like-for-like, with Fragrance and Fashion remaining its largest business segment.

One of the most valuable lessons was that evolving an existing platform can often be harder than designing something new. Working within established systems, design patterns, technical constraints and multiple stakeholder agendas requires deep alignment, diplomacy and strategic clarity.

Much of the project’s success came from speaking to stakeholders individually before defining the direction. Those conversations surfaced assumptions, ambitions, misalignments and shared needs that workshops alone would not have revealed.   Much of the project’s success came from treating strategy as an active part of design. Teams can choose whether to invest in strategic thinking, specialist talent, better tools and the time needed to connect rigour with imagination. But they cannot avoid the strategic consequences of their choices. Every design decision shapes an outcome, whether it is intentional or not. The real question is whether teams actively own those outcomes with clear-sighted intent. Or not.

Most importantly, the project reinforced that digital commerce is not just a set of pages, features or conversion points. It is the way different workstreams come together to express a brand’s intelligence, body language and intent. When strategy, UX, content, data and design are properly connected, the experience starts to feel less transactional and more relational. For luxury brands, that coherence is what makes digital interactions feel human, desirable and true to the brand.

rows.C: Designing a digital companion for the world’s largest retail destination
rows.E: The Dubai Mall was preparing for a major expansion, with more than 160 luxury and premium brands joining Fashion Avenue. But this was not simply a shopping centre. It was a city-scale destination of retail, dining, entertainment, services and attractions. The brief was to redesign the website and app around how people actually experienced it.
rows.F: Most mall websites feel like directories. They tell you what exists, but not how to enjoy the place. The Dubai Mall needed something more useful. Visitors were arriving with different levels of intent, familiarity and confidence. Some wanted inspiration. Some needed parking. Some wanted brands, restaurants, cinema, attractions or simply a way out.
rows.G: Create a digital experience that helped visitors plan before arrival, navigate during their visit, and discover more while on-site. The work needed to turn real user insights into a clear experience architecture, content structure, navigation model and high-fidelity prototype for both the app and website.

rows.L:
1.- EMPATHISE

Understanding the mall through the visitor’s eyes

<TDM_2>

To empathise we wanted more than just interviews, we wanted the purest form of behavioural insights, we wanted to understand the experience of being inside The Dubai Mall without distorting people’s behaviour. Traditional interviews could only tell us what people remembered afterwards. But a place of this scale is experienced moment by moment. People drift, stop, search, ask, follow signs, get distracted, change their mind and often forget the small frictions that shaped their visit.

So we created a contextual research method that felt closer to a family holiday video than a formal study.

Participants were given a small incentive, such as cinema tickets, and a video camera to record their visit naturally. They were not asked to complete tasks. They were asked to behave as they normally would and capture the visit as it unfolded. Afterwards, we interviewed them while reviewing the footage together.

This gave us a more honest, first-hand view of the mall experience throug their eyes. We could see what caught people’s attention, where they hesitated, what they searched for, how they used signposts, when they relied on their mobile phones, and where the experience became frustrating.

One tourist family, for example, arrived through the main entrance as first-time visitors. They had discovered The Dubai Mall through Google while searching for the biggest things to see in Dubai. They were coming from a family holiday in Thailand and were immediately impressed by the scale of Dubai. But once inside, they had no clear plan. They started walking, used an iPad to search for brands, followed signs towards the aquarium, and slowly built their visit through a mixture of curiosity, necessity and chance.

This kind of insights where key for us to feel confident that we were designing stuff that actually mattered.

Visitors weren’t always behaving like shoppers. Sometimes they behaved like tourists. Sometimes like families. Sometimes like commuters. Sometimes like lost pedestrians inside a very beautiful, very complex building.

The research helped us move beyond generic personas and understand the changing mindsets people brought into the mall.


2.- DEFINE

Turning observation into experience models

<TDM_3>

The footage, interviews, focus groups and stakeholder conversations were synthesised into a set of models that helped the team understand the destination from the visitor’s perspective.

We created ‘cultural models’ to show how different customer segments perceived The Dubai Mall. For some, it was a luxury shopping destination. For others, it was a tourist attraction, a family day out, an entertainment venue, a place to eat, or simply something impressive to see while in Dubai.

We also created ‘flow models’ to understand how people moved through the mall. These showed where visitors arrived, how they made decisions, when they changed direction, what information they relied on, and where the experience started to break down.

One of the clearest findings was surprisingly practical.

The mall is so big that people actually struggled to leave.

The mall was highly effective at attracting people in and keeping them engaged, but many visitors became frustrated when they needed to find exits, parking areas, taxis or familiar landmarks. This often happened at the end of an otherwise positive visit, which made it even more important.

Finding the way out was not a small utility problem. It was part of the emotional memory of the experience, and this insight became foundational to how we approached the navigational patter, functional features and content strucutre of the app, it completely shifted the role of the app. It could not simply be a promotional tool or content newsfeed. It needed to behave like a companion. Something that helped visitors discover, decide, move, recover and exit with confidence.


3.- IDEATE

Designing around usabily, convinience and intent, not just departments.

<TDM_4>

From the research, I mapped needs into scenarios, user stories and experience opportunities. Visitors might have arrived wanting inspiration, then need directions, then look for food, then check cinema listings, then find parking, then search for an exit. Their needs didn’t happen in neat categories. They happen in constant motion.

This ‘In-motion’ insight became a core design principle. I.e: the app needed to support quick shifts in intent without making users restart their journey each time.

We explored features around wayfinding, search, parking, services, offers, events, attractions, self-guided tours, brand discovery and location-based prompts. But the value was not in the feature list itself. The value was in understanding when each feature became useful. Search, for example, needed to work across brand, product, location and activity. Wayfinding needed to support more than a destination. It needed to help people understand where they were, what was nearby and how to get back to important points such as exits, parking and concierge desks.

We also explored how beacon technology could add contextual value inside the mall. Rather than interrupting visitors with generic messages, location-based prompts could support discovery at relevant moments, surfacing nearby attractions, offers, services or orientation cues as people moved through the space.

The website and app also had different roles.

The website was more useful for planning, inspiration and pre-visit discovery. The app was more useful during the visit, when people needed practical help, navigation, nearby information and live support. This distinction helped shape the experience architecture across both platforms.


4.- ORGANISE

Orchestrating the content, features and functionality into an easy to ‘get’ experience. 

<TDM_5>

The information architecture had to make hundreds of stores, restaurants, attractions, services, events and facilities feel manageable. More than a navigation problem, it was a content orchestration challenge.

I used the cultural and flow models, user personas, user stories, card sorting and stakeholder input to define the structure of the app and website. Not only the sitemap and content mapping, but also the hierarchy of content based on their experience purpose.

For the website, we created a content matrix that mapped content requirements across key templates. This helped define what each page needed to do, what content it required, and how it supported the wider experience.

For the app, we developed an interaction pattern that made key functions easy to access without relying on a heavy menu. The model allowed users to scroll vertically to explore content, while using horizontal movement to discover related items and functions. This gave the experience a simple rhythm: move down to go deeper, move sideways to discover more.

The interaction pattern was important because the app needed to hold many functions without feeling complicated as you’ll see in the following design stage.

<TDM_6>


5.- PROTOTYPES AND DESIGNS

Making the interaction model tangible

<TDM_7>

<TDM_8>

<TDM_9>

High-fidelity prototypes were created to test the main experience patterns across the app and website.

A key focus was the app navigation model. The challenge was to let users move between functions quickly, without hiding everything inside a traditional menu or making people swipe endlessly through too many options.

We explored a horizontal discovery model with free scroll, momentum and snap behaviour. This allowed users to move through content and functions in a more fluid way, while still keeping the interface controlled and understandable.

The prototypes also included onboarding and tutorial messages for first-time users. These were designed to make the app feel immediately usable without over-explaining the system.

We also created functional annotations to describe how specific interactions should work. This included navigation behaviour, scroll states, content transitions, beacon-triggered notifications, and the logic behind key moments in the experience.

This was important because the work needed to move beyond concept. The design had to be specific enough for product, technology and implementation teams to understand how the experience should behave.

We also tested for other languages, specially for Arabic language requirements using high-fidelity wireframes. This meant checking copy length, layout impact and right-to-left interaction patterns. It was not enough to translate the interface. The experience needed to work structurally for local language behaviour.

<TDM_10>

<TDM_11>

<TDM_12>


6.- IMPLEMENT AND TEST

Refining the experience through use

<TDM_13>

We created usability testing scenarios and activities to understand how people used the prototype in realistic situations.

The test scenarios reflected the kinds of behaviours we had seen in research: finding a brand, locating an attraction, discovering what was new, checking offers, finding parking information, using wayfinding, and recovering from moments of confusion.

The testing helped us refine the navigation model, especially the balance between vertical exploration and horizontal discovery. We adjusted the behaviour so users could move through functions with less effort, while still understanding where they were inside the experience.

Testing also helped validate the value of practical features that might otherwise have seemed secondary, such as exits, parking, nearby services and contextual directions.

In implementation testing and feedback, we reviewed prototype behaviour, interaction details and functional requirements to make sure the intended experience was being translated correctly. This included checking motion, content hierarchy, navigation behaviour, language adaptation and the relationship between modules.

The process gave stakeholders confidence that the experience was not simply attractive, but usable, structured and grounded in real visitor behaviour.
rows.M:
<TDM_14>

At the beginning, it would have been easy to treat The Dubai Mall as a large directory problem. Hundreds of stores. Many categories. Many pages. A lot of information to organise.

But the way we focused our work on research changed everythig we though we were goind for. 

People do not experience a destination through its content structure. They experience it through needs, moods, companions, time pressure, curiosity and fatigue. Visitors wanted to be surprised, but they also want to feel in control. My work was to make that complexity feel navigable.

The contextual research method was especially important because it helped us see behaviour as it happened, not as people reconstructed it later. Giving participants cameras allowed us to observe small but meaningful moments that would have been missed in a standard interview.

One of the simplest insights became one of the most useful. Helping people leave the mall mattered. Not because leaving is glamorous, but because the end of a journey shapes how people remember the whole experience. A destination can be impressive, entertaining and commercially powerful, but if people feel lost at the end, the experience loses some of its care.

This project reinforced a belief that still guides my work. A good digital experience does not just expose information. It understands the situation someone is in and helps them move through it with more confidence.

For The Dubai Mall, that meant designing an app and website that could support both discovery and utility. Something that could inspire a visit, guide a journey, surface what was nearby, help people find what they came for, and quietly step in when the scale of the destination became too much.

In that sense, the work was not only about designing a digital product for a mall. It was about understanding the behavioural layer of a wonderully complex journey and place.

rows.C: Designing The Fourth’s experience by first imagining the brand as a human conversation.
rows.E:
The Fourth is London’s first postnatal care concierge, created to put mothers back at the centre during the fourth trimester.

The service brings together doula care, restorative nourishment, bodywork, reflexology, cleaning, and access to trusted medical professionals. But the real idea is much simpler: mothers should not be expected to recover alone.

The project challenge was helping the founder differentiate and translate a very human purpose into an experience that could feel clear, differentiated and emotionally intelligent across every touchpoint.
rows.F: In May 2026, The Fourth needed my help to identify new workstreams that would help explain a new kind of postnatal care without making care feel like a product. A normal website structure felt too transactional for something this personal, so I started somewhere else: with a conversation. By asking how the brand would speak, listen, explain, reassure and hold back if there were no interface at all, I could map the emotional order of the experience before turning it into pages, touchpoints and interactions.
rows.G: The goal was to help the founder see the full experience The Fourth needed to provide before focusing on any single channel. By mapping its touchpoints, behaviours and moments of trust, we could define where the brand needed to explain, reassure, guide or hold back, creating a clearer foundation for a service that feels transparent, useful and emotionally considered.

rows.L:
1.- PLANNING THE APPROACH

Finding a method to shape a new care experience around the founder’s vision of putting mothers back at the centre.

<F_2>

Before coming up with ideas, or mapping content and features, I needed a way to understand the founder’s vision without jumping straight into pages, channels or content formats. I started thinking about the experience like a decision path, closer to a service flow or a choose-your-own-adventure book, where every moment asks someone to understand something, feel something, or choose what happens next.

That led me to language. If services are built around human choices, then the way a brand speaks, asks, explains and reassures becomes part of the experience itself. For The Fourth, this felt especially important because the heart of the service is already human conversation: a mother speaking to someone who listens, guides and helps her make sense of the support she needs.

So I stripped the experience back to its simplest form: no website, no interface, no content plan. Just a conversation. If the brand was a person, what would it say first? What would it ask? When would it explain, reassure, guide or give someone space? That became the starting point for Conversational Design.


2.- EMPATHISE

Starting with the founder, not the interface.

<F_3>

I started by speaking with Lauren about why and how The Fourth needed to exist.

The conversation focused on understanding the founder’s point of view as someone with lived experience, care knowledge and a clear ambition to create something that did not yet exist. The conversation was less about functional requirements and more about the reality she was trying to respond to: the lack of structured maternal care after birth, the emotional and physical vulnerability of recovery, and the way the mother often becomes secondary once the baby arrives. That helped define the emotional centre of the experience.

The Fourth was not simply offering services. It was saying: “You are still the person who needs care.” This insight mattered because it changed how the experience needed to behave.

I recorded the conversation and used Otter.ai to transcribe it into text. This turned the conversation into material I could return to, study and break down more carefully. It also allowed me to capture the actual words, instincts and priorities behind the founder’s vision, rather than translating everything too quickly into design assumptions.


3.- DEFINE

Turning the conversation into an experience logic

<F_4>

Once the conversation was transcribed, I used a Claude skill I had created to help analyse the material. The purpose was not to let the tool define the experience for me, but to help identify early patterns, decision paths, experience stages and possible touchpoints hidden inside the conversation.

This gave me a first working map. It helped reveal how The Fourth might move someone from not knowing what support they need, to having a clearer idea, to considering care, and finally to feeling ready to decide.

That became the centre of gravity for the experience: moving mothers towards certainty. Not by pushing them through a funnel, but by helping each moment build clarity, trust and emotional permission.


4.- MAP

Mapping touchpoints by purpose, behaviour and channel.

<F_5>

I then turned the early analysis into a touchpoint map. For each moment, I looked at the channel, the purpose and the behaviour the brand needed to express. This included moments across the website, social, consultation, WhatsApp, email, onboarding, care delivery and aftercare.

The map helped clarify what each part of the experience was actually for. Some moments needed to explain. Some needed to reassure. Some needed to ask better questions. Some needed to make support feel normal. Some simply needed to hold space.

This made the experience easier to orchestrate. Instead of thinking only in pages or features, we could see the role each touchpoint played in helping someone move from uncertainty to confidence.

<F_6>


5.- IDEATE

Using the map to identify what to build next.

<F_7>

Once the touchpoints were clear, I compiled the purpose and description of each moment and used that as the basis for ideation. This helped us generate ideas that were connected to the experience, rather than just adding features because they sounded useful.

The ideas included a more guided consultation journey, a clearer postnatal needs assessment, more personal onboarding, a stronger WhatsApp support layer, useful content around recovery, referral moments that transfer trust, and aftercare that continues the relationship beyond the first service delivery.

The map also helped the founder and I review and prioritise ideas based on how foundational they were to the experience and how desirable they felt. It also revealed new opportunities for user research, especially around the moments where trust, clarity or reassurance mattered most.
rows.M:
<F_8>

A lot of UX work begins with user needs, pain points and value propositions. Those things matter, and this work created clear next steps for that kind of research, testing and design. But The Fourth also needed something more foundational: a way to understand how the a new kind of experience should relate to people before deciding what to research and build next. And this became the real value of the process. By treating the experience as a conversation, language became more than tone of voice. It became a way to reveal desired structure. What the brand has to say, what it wants to ask, how it reassures, when it explains, and when it gives space all became design decisions. Not just content or functional decisions.

This helped define the body language of the brand across touchpoints. The experience needed to feel coherent not only as a journey, but as a presence. A mother should feel the same care, restraint and clarity whether she is reading the website, speaking to someone on WhatsApp, completing an assessment, receiving a proposal or moving into aftercare.

That feels especially relevant now, in a world where more experiences will be shaped by language, AI agents and conversational interfaces. The question that can empower founders and creaters is not only what can a brand automate or personalise. It is what kind of relationship is the brand creating through every interaction?

With this work, The Fourth uncovered the idea of putting the mom’s back at the center as a key relational idea, the insight wasn’t blindly focused on efficiency for the sake of efficiency. It was to make every interaction feel considered, more transparent and more human. The structure had to guide the mother towards certainty, while the language carried the nuance, empathy and trust that made the service feel less transactional and more like it ‘gets’ you.
